text: At nine on Thursday, the general contractor called Dokgo Chul in the Guro foundation pit. He was already counting minutes.
Dokgo had seven hours before handover. He bowed to the phone and promised they were on schedule. The smile vanished when he hung up.
He passed the deadline to the eight porters below him. They had seven hours, and the general contractor was counting every minute.
Ryu Survey set up beside the C-grade gate. Taeo regretted researching that grade the night before.
Nib's compulsory hard hat perched on his ears. Haein drilled two holes through it, making room for them. Nib approved the result. He still refused boots.
Haein's cable now carried radio signals through the gate, provided it stayed intact. Taeo would log Nib's calls. Minho reminded him, again, to stay outside.
Dokgo demanded the scout enter at ten sharp. Minho insisted Nib would enter when the frame had been checked. Dokgo answered with the contract.
His third-tier subcontract imposed five million won per hour for late handover. Dokgo passed the general contractor's delay charges to his workers.
His porter app counted down to four o'clock. Taeo calculated the penalty at eighty-three thousand, three hundred and thirty-three won every minute.
Gu Dami caught Taeo recognising her from the news. She said the cameras had filmed the hunters, and only her back.
Dami knew Dokgo's claim about the missing porter. She needed his work: Bluebird wanted an instalment tomorrow, and she owed two million, one hundred thousand won.
She'd borrowed for draws at eighteen and received two commons, leased to a warehouse for thirty thousand won each monthly. The interest had pulled better than she had.
Nib had been studying her vest with intense admiration. Fourteen pockets, he counted. Dami corrected him: sixteen. There were two more inside.
Nib earned sixty thousand won daily. Dami earned ninety thousand without insurance. Taeo earned nothing and stayed outside. Dami called that lucky.
The word landed harder than Taeo expected. A single minute of the lateness penalty cost almost as much as Dami earned for an entire day.
Dokgo announced the order: scout, then porters, then Ironclad Seven at three. 'The cheap ones go first.' Dami and Nib exchanged a look.
Dami introduced her partner, fifty-eight-year-old Kwak Mansu. He called Nib son and recommended knee pads for the low galleries. Nib answered, 'I'm short.'
Kwak's laugh became a wheezing cough. Dami demanded his inhaler. He said it was in his jacket, followed by the familiar reassurance: it was fine.
Quietly, he asked her not to mention his asthma near Dokgo. Dokgo didn't pick wheezers for work.
Taeo watched him hang up the jacket, the blue inhaler cap visible in its pocket. Grandpa said it was fine too.
At ten, the contractor called again: six hours left. Minho pointed at Taeo, then at his chair. The instruction hadn't changed.
Nib entered first, carrying his radio beside the cable. A white return mark formed on his wrist as he crossed. Minho had requested nothing clever.
Taeo lurched sideways and grabbed the table. He felt the ground tilt. Haein steadied the equipment and explained that their ground hadn't moved. He had felt Nib's.
Nib confirmed that the ground inside sloped left. The sensation had lasted three seconds before Taeo lost him again.
Taeo checked his nose and asked whether he was bleeding. Haein inspected him with interest. Her answer was reassuring only briefly: 'Not yet.'
Beyond Nib stretched a quarry of slanted stone terraces and dark galleries beneath a green dusk sky. Even the distant horizon leaned left.
Ryu's crew and mule went ahead, then the porters crossed with their loads. Dami wore number seven. Her partner Kwak wore eight. Each person received a return mark.
Outside, Taeo rested his hand against the steel frame. His knuckles curled, ready for the old signal, but he didn't knock.
At eleven, Dokgo's phone rang again. Five hours remained. He bowed to it repeatedly, promising obedience while the clock above him kept running.
Taeo logged Nib's warnings about loose stone while Haein worked on equipment. Waiting hadn't become easier. Taeo had only become quieter.
At noon, the forward camp was twenty minutes behind. The contractor put the penalty at ₩1,666,666. Dokgo promised to fix it.
He seized the survey handset despite Haein's objection. His order split the porter pairs. Even numbers would take the lower gallery.
Minho warned that the route was unsurveyed. Dokgo answered that it was forty metres shorter. Since it wasn't on Ryu's survey line, he considered it outside their responsibility.
Taeo half rose, ready to say something. The words didn't come. He watched Dokgo without speaking.
Minho ordered his crew to tape both ends of the lower gallery. The hazard would be marked, even as the porters were sent through it.
Dami offered to take the lower route instead. Kwak told her she was faster on the upper run. He ducked beneath the warning tape and disappeared into the dark.
At one, the phone rang again. Three hours remained, and the job was still behind. Dokgo called roll, one through eight.
At the forward camp, number six answered. Asked for seven, Dami gave her name and location. Nib was already looking toward the lower gallery's exit.
Eight didn't answer. Dokgo called again, this time using Kwak Mansu's name. Nib reported that Kwak had never reached the forward camp.
Outside, Kwak's jacket still hung on its hook. The blue inhaler cap was still in the pocket, right where Taeo had seen it.
Dami said Kwak had entered the lower gallery alone at half past twelve. Taeo went pale as he listened.
Dokgo looked at his countdown. Less than three hours remained. Every minute still carried the same price.
Inside, Dami and Nib stared into the black gallery while other porters shouldered their loads. Dokgo's voice came through the relay: 'He's resting somewhere. Keep moving.'
